sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Xipe** ​(*xipe*) — ‌Spring, Agriculture, ‌Flayed · ​The ​flayed one ​— belongs ​to the ​Nahuatl ‌tradition, where ​it is ​catalogued under ‌the domain ​"Spring, ‌Agriculture, Flayed". ​The name ‌means "The ​flayed ​one"[^1].

**Xipe** ​— Xipe ​Tōtec, 'Our ​Lord ‌the Flayed ​One' — ‌is the ​Mexica ‌god of ​**spring, agriculture, ‌and renewal** ​whose ‌priests wore ​the flayed ​skins of ‌sacrificial captives ‌for ‌twenty days. ​Beneath the ​terror lay ‌a ​farming theology: ​as the ‌maize seed ​sheds ​its husk ‌to sprout, ​so the ‌god ​sheds his ​skin to ​feed the ​world. ‌He was ‌also patron ​of goldsmiths ‌and ​lord of ​the west.[^2]

‌PuniCodex records ‌the canonical ‌scholarly ‌spelling **Xipe** ​and serves ‌its temple ​at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/xipe/). ​The displayed ‌form is ​ASCII-equivalent ​— a ​description computed ‌from the ​displayed ​form itself. ​The plain ‌ASCII form ​*xipe* ‌contains the ​same letters: ‌no recovered ​diacritics or ‌special ‌encoding is ​claimed. The ​work here ​is ​consistent citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
The ​name ‌is attested ‌in ​the ​colonial alphabetic ​corpus ​and ​in logographic ‌writing ​in ​the ‌codices; the ​restoration ‌uses ​the normalized ‌scholarly ​orthography. ​Etymologically ​the name ​means ​"The ‌flayed one"[^1].

​The ‌canonical ​spelling **Xipe** ‌matches ​the ‌conventional ​scholarly romanization. ‌The ​plain ​ASCII form ‌*xipe* ‌contains ‌the ​same letters, ​so ‌no ​lost diacritics ​or ‌encoding ​transition is ​claimed. ‌The ​editorial ‌work is ​to ​fix ​one reviewed ​reference ‌spelling, ‌preserve capitalization ​and ‌provenance, ​and ​keep the ‌original ‌evidence ‌visible. The ‌displayed ​form ‌is ​ASCII-equivalent — ​a ​description ‌computed from ​the ​displayed ​form itself.

‌The ​letter-by-letter ​transformation ​runs:

- **x** ‌→ ​**X** ‌— Same
- ​**i** ‌→ ​**i** ‌— Same
- ‌**p** ​→ ​**p** — ​Same
- ​**e** ‌→ **e** ‌— ​Same

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/xipe/** ​— ​Restored ​scholarly ‌form.

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**xipe** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Xipe.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Xipe" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "Xipe" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"xipe" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

​The ​pronunciation ‌given above ‌reconstructs ​the ‌sound ​world in ​which ‌Xipe ‌was invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not a ​performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌reconstructed pronunciation ​of ‌Xipe ​is explained ‌separately ‌from ​its ​conventional Latin ​spelling, ​which ‌adds no ‌diacritic ​marks.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌Xipe ‌place ​spring, agriculture, ​flayed ​at ​the center ​of ‌a living ​mythological ​world.

### ‌Origins (Myth)

​Xipe ‌appears ​in nahuatl ‌tradition ​as spring, ​agriculture, ​flayed. ​The name's ​meaning, ‌"The ​flayed one", ‌shapes ​the narratives ‌told ​about ‌this figure.

### ​Worship ‌and ​Memory (Cult)

​Devotees ‌and later ‌tradition-keepers ‌preserved ​Xipe in ​ritual, ‌text, ​and iconography, ​ensuring ‌the name ​survived ​into ‌the modern ​scholarly ‌record.

​The myths ​of ​Xipe survive ​in ‌fragments, ‌summaries, and ​later ‌retellings. ​Each version ​reflects ‌the interests ‌of ‌its ‌tellers — ​poets, ‌priests, ​philosophers, and ​scholars. ​The PuniCodex ‌entry ​does ​not privilege ​a ‌single ​version; it ​gathers ​the attestations ‌so ​that ‌readers can ​compare ‌them. ​The restoration ‌Xipe ‌gives the ​figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or ​artifact in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet ​assigned to ‌Xipe ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should ​be read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Nahuatl ​name ‌of ​this ‌type the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ​be ‌thin, and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains ‌the ​textual ​testimony gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources ​section.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Xipe, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​spring ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Xipe ​Tōtec asks ‌the question ‌every ​farmer knows ​and every ​city ​forgets: what ​must die ‌for ​something else ​to live? ‌His ​answer is ‌a skin. ​The ‌maize seed ​does not ​negotiate ​with its ​husk; it ​splits ‌it. The ​god ‌does not ​sympathize with ‌the ​covering; he ‌wears it. ​In ‌a culture ​that now ​separates ‌death from ‌dinner by ‌an ​almost perfectly ​opaque supply ‌chain, ​the Flayed ​One insists ‌on ​the connection: ​your bread ‌was ​once a ‌seed's corpse, ​your ​gold was ​once a ​stone's ‌wound.

To ‌meditate on ​Xipe ‌is to ​meditate on ​the ‌cost of ‌renewal. He ‌is ‌not a ​god of ‌resurrection ​— nothing ​in the ​rite ‌promises the ​flayed ​man his ​life back. ‌He ​is a ​god of ​**transfer**: ‌life moves, ​and something ‌is ​always left ‌behind. The ​friars ‌saw only ‌cruelty; the ​Mexica ​saw the ​farming year. ​Both ‌were reading ‌the same ​skin.[^1]
